newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan may tender Caspian oil areas in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan may tender Caspian oil areas in 1997.

text.p: Kazakhstan, sitting on some of the world's largest offshore oil and gas reserves, may hold tenders for energy blocks in its continental shelf of the Caspian Sea by the end of 1997, a top Kazakh energy official said on Wednesday.

Baltabek Kuandykov, president of state-owned KazakhstanCaspiyShelf (KCS), which is working with an international consortium of the same name in the Kazakh sector of the Caspian, said consortium members would have first pick at blocks but that other companies could bid.

"We are preparing to hold tenders for shelf reserves and will offer blocks to investors after consortium members select their own blocks, maybe by the end of 1997," Kuandykov told a news conference at an international oil and gas conference.
"This (Kazakh offshore reserves) will be comparable in scale to the North Sea projects."
He gave no details on tender terms, but said that state-owned KCS -- which holds a general license for Kazakh shelf reserves -- would take part in future output.

The KazakhstanCaspiyShelf (KCS) consortium includes Agip SpA of Italy, the British Petroleum /Den Norske Stats Oljeselskap AS (Statoil) alliance, Total of France, U.S. Mobil Corp, Royal Dutch/Shell and British Gas Plc.
State-owned KCS is not now a consortium member.
The consortium was set up in 1993 to chart over 100,000 square km (38,600 square miles) of unexplored territory in what has been called the world's largest offshore oil search.
Kazakhstan has said that only six percent of the entire survey area will be handed over to the KCS consortium -- leaving big reserves for other foreign energy investors.

Kazakhstan said in June that a seismic survey of its continental shelf put reserves at a possible 10 billion tonnes of crude oil and two trillion cubic metres of natural gas. The numbers, if confirmed, dwarf Russia's total proven crude oil reserves of around 6.7 billion tonnes.
State-owned KCS and McDermott International Inc of the United States said they had completed an infrastructure feasibility study on the onshore facilities needed to support offshore development.
The study is an important prelude to the tenders, since multiple foreign investors need common solutions to expensive issues like transport, processing and other infrastructure.

McDermott Vice-President Richard Ward told the same briefing that the study assumed an early production target for Kazakh offshore reserves of around 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) from three well-head platforms by 2004, rising to around 1.2 million bpd from eight platforms by 2013.

Kuandykov said the KCS consortium plans to drill its first well in 1998, but it must still negotiate production-sharing contracts with the Kazakh government once the consortium's seismic survey work is completed early next year.
He said initial infrastructure costs, both offshore and onshore, could total $12-$15 billion.
Facilities needing refurbishment or greenfield construction include pipelines, tanker berths, platforms, special compressor facilities, power generators and social infrastructure.

Kazakhstan's continental shelf is divided into two zones -- a northern, shallow water area with high-sulphur crude requiring expensive, non-traditional recovery technologies, and a southern area with deeper water that does not freeze and may be less costly to produce.
